title: Nina and the Secret Thanks
markdown:
Nina was a tiny mouse, no bigger than a thumb, whiskers that wiggled at almost everything. She lived in a kitchen that smelled of warm bread and cinnamon, full of cozy spots. Her very best friend was Toffee, a tabby plush, soft as a dandelion puff, shiny button eyes, a gentle quiet way. He was her constant companion, warm and furry at her side.

Their days were mostly peaceful. Nina scurried for the tastiest crumbs from the baker’s table, behind the flour tin, along the warm skirting. Toffee sat nearby, content among the smells, a soft landmark she could always find. Their favourite thing, the absolute best part of the day, was the big bread basket. Crusty bread filled it — rye, and a pale loaf, and sometimes a heel still warm. Nina nibbled a little, always leaving plenty, and Toffee sat beside it, button eyes seeming to sparkle at the aroma.

Then something strange began. One sunny morning Nina looked at the basket, nose twitching as usual, and found something unexpected. Tucked beside a thick crusty slice of rye, peeking from under a crust, was a tiny folded paper. She unfolded it with little paws. The paper rustled. In a wobbly minuscule script like tiny dancing ants: Thank you for the bread. It was so yummy.

Nina blinked, bead-bright eyes, head tilting. “Toffee. Who left this?” Toffee blinked his button eyes back, silent and steady. A quiver ran through her whiskers. A moth-wing flutter in her tummy. A new creature in their lovely safe kitchen?

Nina could feel a little flutter of worry. Her curiosity was always bigger and brighter, a sunshine beam that chased shadows. She really wanted to know who was thanking them. “We must find out.” She nudged Toffee, a tiny bump of plush. He gave a soft plush nod.

They usually stayed very close to the warm kitchen, their safe haven of familiar sights and comforting sounds. The world outside the window smelled of damp earth and sweet flowers. It was also bigger. Nina, brave about crumbs, always felt nervous about stepping too far. She might get lost. The garden might be too big, and she might not find her way back. Her whiskers drooped at the mere suggestion.

The baker only left the little door open a short while each morning. If they did not go now, the chance would be gone. Nina puffed her little chest. Toffee a reassuring weight against her side, she nudged the back door. Click. Not loud. Not startling. The sound of leaving. Fresh cool air, damp earth, sweet flowers. A new place. Exciting. A little wobbly.

“Come on, Toffee.” Her whiskers twitched with a new buzz, all the way to her paws. They followed the faint scent of breadcrumbs along the step, then into the first wet grass. They found paw prints so small they looked like dots, leading away from the basket toward the garden. Much smaller than Nina’s own. A print on a leaf. A print in a crumb of mud. Following the tiny trail was like finding a single fallen star in a field of flowers. It required close attention. Her tummy did a flip-flop. Toffee’s plush foot caught on a stem; she waited while he tugged free.

The prints disappeared near a big green mossy stone, a small hill to Nina. She stopped. Her heart thumped a soft drum. The garden was a vast green expanse, tall blades swaying. For a moment the old whisper came: maybe too much, maybe back to the safe kitchen. Toffee nudged her, plush side an anchor. She was not alone.

Then she spotted it — a single perfect breadcrumb, glinting in a stray sunbeam, leading around the mossy stone. The worry did not vanish. Her determination grew, a tiny spark fanned warm. She kept going, Toffee at her side. They were learning to read the tiny signs, little detectives of the garden.

And then they saw them. Peeking from behind wildflowers of red, blue, and yellow, a whole family of field mice, gathering fallen seeds and bits of grain. Beside their little nest sat a miniature bread basket, just like Nina and Toffee’s, filled with tiny pieces. The littlest field mouse held one of the thank-you notes, smoothing it with a tiny paw.

“They’re the ones.” Nina’s whiskers danced. The field mice were just as surprised and happy. They explained, in chirpy voices, that they often found dropped bread near the kitchen window, perhaps from busy hands, and wanted to show their appreciation.

Nina and Toffee had found the generous little bakers. How do you thank someone for thanking you? Nina looked at Toffee, mind whirring. “We have some of our very favourite cheese crumbs. The bestest crumbs in the whole kitchen. Maybe they’d like them even more.” Toffee gave a soft plush sigh. He knew how she had carefully saved them. She looked at the busy field mice, noses twitching with hope. With a big brave breath she placed the golden crumbs down. Sharp cheese-scent filled the air. Her tiny paws on the soft earth seemed very loud. A sharing of her very favourite thing.

The field mice squeaked with delight, a happy chorus. They gathered the crumbs with cheerful speed. They waved tiny paws. Nina waved back, heart light and full. Toffee’s button eyes shone with quiet approval.

They turned toward the familiar kitchen. The garden did not seem quite so big. The tall grass was only grass. The mossy stone was a place they had passed. At their own door Nina paused. A tiny echo of the earlier flutter tickled her whiskers. Then she remembered the happy squeaks and the scent of shared cheese. She nudged the door. With Toffee beside her she stepped into warmth, baking bread, comfort. The memory lingered like a second loaf, still warm, and the next morning she left a little extra rye where a tiny note might find it.
